pages.student_title: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo
pages.subtitle: The second California mission, built on the homeland of the Rumsen and Esselen peoples. Saint Junípero Serra lived and is buried here.
pages.founding_source_note: Society of Architectural Historians, SAH Archipedia, "Carmel Mission"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission San Carlos Borromeo.
pages.intro: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo is often called Carmel Mission. Saint Junípero Serra founded it in 1770. It was the second California mission and the main office for all the others. It stands on the homeland of the Rumsen and Esselen peoples. Its story includes faith and a beautiful stone church. It also includes sickness and great loss for the Native people who lived there.
story_paragraphs: Long before the Spanish came, the Rumsen people lived around Monterey Bay and the Carmel River. Their neighbors, the Esselen, lived in the mountains and along the rocky coast to the south. The Esselen Tribe says its people have lived there for more than 6,000 years.

On June 3, 1770, Father Junípero Serra founded Mission San Carlos Borromeo next to the Spanish fort at Monterey. It was the second California mission. About a year later, he moved it about five miles south, near the Carmel River. The new place had fresh water all year and better land for farming.
Serra made Carmel his home. From there he led all the California missions. He died at the mission on August 28, 1784, and was buried in the church.

Rumsen and Esselen people were brought into the mission and baptized. By the end of 1778, the five Rumsen villages nearby were empty. Mission life was very hard. People had to work for the mission and follow its rules. The Esselen Tribe says families were separated, and people were not allowed to speak their own languages or keep their traditions.
Sickness spread quickly at the mission. A measles outbreak in 1806 was one of the worst. In 1795, about 876 Native people lived there. By 1834, only 188 were left.
Father Fermín Lasuén led the missions after Serra. He had a new church built of stone. A master stonemason named Manuel Ruiz led the work, and the church was dedicated in 1797.

In 1834, the Mexican government took the missions away from the Church. The buildings stood empty, and in the early 1850s the church roof fell in. In 1884, a priest named Angelo Casanova gave the church a new roof. In the 1930s, a builder named Harry Downie began careful repairs that lasted for many years.
Today, the mission is a parish church and a basilica. The Rumsen and Esselen people are still here too. Their tribes are working to bring back their languages and to care for their homelands.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: Two Native peoples lived at this mission. The Rumsen, who are one of the Ohlone peoples, came from villages such as Achasta, near Monterey and the Carmel River. The Esselen came from the mountains and coast to the south. By 1794, about three out of four people at the mission were Rumsen, and one out of four was Esselen. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land, language, and freedom. Some people resisted. In 1779, a mission leader named Baltazar ran away and gathered others to stand against the mission. Several tribes today come from the families of the people of this mission. They include the Ohlone Costanoan Esselen Nation, the Esselen Tribe of Monterey County, and the Costanoan Rumsen Carmel Tribe.
type_specific.mission_life: Carmel was the headquarters of the California missions for more than 30 years, so letters, reports, and visitors came here from all the other missions. The mission kept a library of about 1,500 books. Beside the church stood a school, workshops, sleeping rooms, and storehouses for grain. The Rumsen and Esselen people who lived at the mission did the daily work. For them, this was a very different life from the one their families had known.
type_specific.architecture: The church is built of brown sandstone, with walls about five feet thick. It has two bell towers that do not match. The bigger one has a rounded dome on top. Over the front door is a window shaped like a star. Inside, the ceiling curves in a tall arch. Not everything you see is from the 1790s. The roof fell in during the 1850s. The tile roof and curved wooden ceiling were rebuilt in the 1930s, and most of the buildings around the courtyard were rebuilt on the old foundations. The stone walls and towers are from the first church.

pages.subtitle: The third California mission, founded in a quiet valley of oak trees on the homeland of the Salinan people.
pages.founding_source_note: Mission San Antonio de Padua, "History"; Monterey County Historical Society, "Mission San Antonio de Padua."
pages.intro: Mission San Antonio de Padua was the third California mission. Saint Junípero Serra founded it in 1771 in a valley full of oak trees. This land is the homeland of the Salinan people. The mission became known for its clever water system and its mill. Its story also includes hunger, sickness, and the loss of language and freedom for the Salinan people.
story_paragraphs: For a very long time, the Salinan people have lived in the valleys, hills, and coast of what are now Monterey and San Luis Obispo Counties. They built villages beside rivers and streams. Acorns were one of their most important foods. They burned the brush under the oak trees so the acorns would be easy to find in the fall.

On July 14, 1771, Father Junípero Serra came to this valley with two other priests, Miguel Pieras and Buenaventura Sitjar. They hung the mission bells on the branch of an oak tree. Serra named the new mission for Saint Anthony of Padua. Then he went on his way, and the two priests stayed to build.

In 1773, the mission moved farther up the valley, because the first spot did not have enough water. A Salinan elder writes that in that same year, a very old Salinan woman came to the mission and asked to be baptized. She was given the name Agata Maria.

The mission grew. By 1776, about 500 people lived there. Workers built dams on the river and sent the water through ditches and clay pipes to the fields. In 1806, they finished a mill where rushing water turned a wheel to grind grain. A large new church was built from 1810 to 1813.

Mission life was hard for the Salinan people. They had to work for the mission and live by its rules. A Salinan elder named Suzanne Pierce Taylor writes that the mission system broke the careful way her people had always shared the land's food, so hunger became more common when rain did not come. People had to speak Spanish, and after a few generations the Salinan language was almost forgotten. New sicknesses spread through the missions, and many Native people died.
In 1834, the government took the mission away from the Church. The last priest died in 1882, and the empty buildings began to fall down.

People started to rebuild the mission in 1903, and a Salinan family, the Encinales, helped. The mission was rebuilt again beginning in 1948. Today, the Salinan people are still here, working to bring back their language and culture.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Salinan people. The Salinan spoke three forms of their language. One was spoken on the coast, one near this mission, and one near Mission San Miguel. They lived in villages led by a headman, and they made choices by talking until everyone agreed. They wove baskets so tight that they could cook in them with hot stones. When the mission came, many Salinan people were baptized. Mission life also brought forced work, strict rules, hunger, sickness, and the loss of land, language, and freedom. A Salinan elder writes, "We do not look the same, dress the same, live the same or speak the same, but we are here."
type_specific.mission_life: People at the mission grew wheat, grapes, and olives, and they raised cattle and horses. At one time the mission had more than 800 horses. Water from the river was used for the fields, for washing, and for the mill that ground grain into flour. The mission bells told everyone when to pray, work, and eat. Salinan people did the farming, building, and herding. Some lived and worked at ranches far from the church.
type_specific.architecture: The church is about 200 feet long, with adobe walls about six feet thick at the bottom. In front of the church is a wall of fired brick with arched openings for three bells. A curved brick passage joins this bell wall to the church door. Very little of what you see is from mission days. By the early 1900s the church was a ruin. Starting in 1948, the church and the buildings around the courtyard were rebuilt, with new adobe bricks made from the dirt of the old fallen walls. Parts of the old water system can still be seen near the mission.

pages.subtitle: The fourth California mission, built on the homeland of the Tongva people near what is now Los Angeles.
pages.founding_source_note: Los Angeles Conservancy, "Mission San Gabriel Arcángel"; California Missions Foundation, "Mission San Gabriel."

quick_facts.label: Founded by
quick_facts.value: Fathers Pedro Cambón and Angel Somera, sent by Saint Junípero Serra

pages.intro: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel was the fourth California mission. Two priests sent by Saint Junípero Serra founded it in 1771. It stands on the homeland of the Tongva people, the first people of the Los Angeles area. The mission grew large and rich in crops. For the Tongva, it also brought forced work, sickness, and the loss of their land. Some of them fought back.
story_paragraphs: The Tongva people are the first people of the Los Angeles area and four islands off its coast. Their nation says its history there goes back about 8,000 years. Around 1770, about 5,000 Tongva lived in more than fifty villages.

On September 8, 1771, two priests named Pedro Cambón and Angel Somera founded Mission San Gabriel Arcángel. Father Serra had sent them. It was the fourth California mission. The first spot was near a river, and it flooded again and again. In 1775, the mission moved to higher ground, where it stands today. That place was the Tongva village of Toviscanga.
In 1781, a group of settlers walked from the mission to start a new town nearby. That town became the city of Los Angeles.

The mission grew quickly. Tongva people from many villages were brought there and baptized. They were made to build the mission, plant the fields, and care for the animals. The National Park Service says they faced violence, too much work, sickness, and too little food. They were not free to hold their own ceremonies and dances.

In 1785, some Tongva decided to fight back. A man named Nicolás José, who lived at the mission, made a plan with a young woman named Toypurina. She was a respected leader from the village of Japchivit. She asked as many as eight villages to join. On the night of October 25, they came to the mission, but someone had warned the soldiers. The soldiers were waiting, and the leaders were caught.

At her trial, Toypurina said she was angry with the priests and the others at the mission because they were living on her people's land. She was sent far away to live at another mission and never came home.
A new church of stone and brick was finished in 1805. In 1834, the government took the mission away from the Church.
In July 2020, a fire destroyed the church roof. The church was repaired and opened again in 2023. Today, the Tongva people still live in the Los Angeles area.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Tongva people. The Spanish called them Gabrielinos, after the mission. Before the mission, the Tongva lived in many separate villages, each with its own leaders. Their homeland covered more than a million acres. The Gabrielino/Tongva Nation says the mission brought "enslavement and abuse of our ancestors." People were made to work, many died from sickness, and the Tongva lost their land. Some resisted, as Toypurina and Nicolás José did in 1785. About 6,000 Native people are buried in the mission cemetery. A wall at the mission now lists the names of 7,054 Native people who were baptized there. Today, Tongva people still live in and around Los Angeles and keep their culture alive.
type_specific.mission_life: San Gabriel was called the "Pride of the Missions" because it grew so much food. Its fields grew more wheat than any other mission, and it had large vineyards of grapes. Tongva workers also made soap, leather, and cloth, and the mission sent soap to other missions. Bells told everyone when to pray, work, and eat. The Tongva did this work because they had to. Their own way of life, in their own villages, had been taken from them.
type_specific.architecture: The church does not look like the other mission churches. A priest named Antonio Cruzado planned it. He came from Córdoba, Spain, and the church looks a little like the great cathedral there. Its long side wall has tall supports called buttresses, with pointed caps on top, and long, narrow windows. The walls are stone below and fired brick above. The first bell tower fell in an earthquake in 1812. A bell wall with six bells was finished in 1828. The walls and bell wall are from mission days. The roof and wooden ceiling are new. They were rebuilt after the fire of 2020.

pages.student_title: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa
pages.subtitle: The fifth California mission, founded in the Valley of the Bears on the homeland of the Northern Chumash people.
pages.founding_source_note: California Missions Foundation, "Mission San Luis Obispo"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission San Luis Obispo.
pages.intro: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa was the fifth California mission. Saint Junípero Serra founded it in 1772 near a place the Spanish called the Valley of the Bears. This land is the homeland of the Northern Chumash people, who have lived here for more than 10,000 years. The mission is known for its red roof tiles. Its story also includes loss for the Chumash people.
story_paragraphs: The Northern Chumash people have lived along this part of the California coast for more than 10,000 years. They had villages from the ocean to the hills. One village, called tiłhini, stood where the city of San Luis Obispo is now. Its name means "place of the full moon."

In 1769, Spanish explorers passed through a nearby valley and saw grizzly bears. They named it the Valley of the Bears. Three years later, the first missions were running out of food. In the summer of 1772, hunters came back to this valley and sent bear meat to the hungry missions. They also traded meat with the local people for seeds to eat.

Father Junípero Serra decided this was a good place for a mission. On September 1, 1772, he founded Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa. It was the fifth California mission. He left the next day, and a priest named José Cavaller stayed to build it.

The first buildings had roofs made of dry reeds. In 1776, a burning arrow landed on a roof, and fire destroyed many buildings. So the priests began making roof tiles out of baked clay, which cannot catch fire. Red clay tiles became a famous part of the California missions.

Many Chumash people were baptized and came to live at the mission. By 1804, 832 lived there. Their lives changed completely. They had to work for the mission and follow its rules, and they were no longer free to live in their own villages in their own way. New sicknesses spread through the missions, and many Native people died.
The church that stands today was built from 1792 to 1794. In 1835, the government took the mission away from the Church, and ten years later the mission lands were sold.

In the 1880s, the old church was covered with wooden boards so it would look like churches in the eastern United States. In the 1930s, a priest named John Harnett took the boards off and rebuilt the bell tower.
Today, the mission is a parish church. The Northern Chumash people still live in their homeland, and they are singing their old songs again.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Northern Chumash people. One tribe of their descendants is called yak tityu tityu yak tiłhini. The name means "the people of the full moon." Their villages reached from the places now called Cambria and Morro Bay to Avila Beach and Nipomo. They fished, gathered abalone and other food from the sea, traded shell beads, and wove baskets with very fine designs. When the mission came, many Chumash people were baptized. Mission life also brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. The last person who grew up speaking the tribe's language was a woman named Rosario Cooper. She shared her words and songs with a visitor who wrote them down between 1912 and 1917. Because of her, the tribe is learning its language again today.
type_specific.mission_life: The mission buildings stood around a square courtyard. The church was on one side, the priests' rooms on another, and workshops and storehouses on the rest. Bells told everyone when to pray, work, and eat. A priest named Luis Antonio Martínez led the mission for 34 years and planted a large vineyard. Chumash people did the farming and building. For them, mission life was a big change from their own way of life.
type_specific.architecture: The church is made of adobe with a roof of clay tiles. It is shaped like the letter L, with a second long room joining the main one at a corner. No other California mission church has this shape. At the front, the bells hang in openings above the entry porch instead of in a separate tower. The three bells were first made in Peru in 1818. The adobe church is from 1792 to 1794, but the front is not. The bell openings and porch were torn down in the 1880s and rebuilt in the 1930s. The inside was repaired in the 1940s, when workers uncovered the old wooden ceiling beams.

canonical.match_title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores)

pages.subtitle: The sixth California mission, often called Mission Dolores, built on the homeland of the Ramaytush Ohlone people in what is now San Francisco.
pages.founding_source_note: Year only, as the missions hub shows it. The mission's own site gives October 9, 1776; other sources give June 29, 1776.
pages.intro: Mission San Francisco de Asís was the sixth California mission. Most people call it Mission Dolores. A priest named Francisco Palóu founded it in 1776 on the homeland of the Ramaytush Ohlone people. Its small adobe church is the oldest building still standing in San Francisco. The mission's story is also one of the saddest, because so many Native people died there.
story_paragraphs: The Ramaytush Ohlone are the first people of the San Francisco Peninsula. Before the Spanish came, there were about 1,500 to 2,000 of them, living in about ten separate tribes. The tribe that lived where the city of San Francisco is now is called the Yelamu today.

In 1776, a Spanish officer named Juan Bautista de Anza led settlers overland from Mexico. He chose one place for a fort and another for a mission. That same year, Father Francisco Palóu, a friend of Father Serra, founded the mission. It was the sixth in California.

The mission was named for Saint Francis of Assisi, who started the Franciscan order. Nearby ran a stream that the Spanish had named for Our Lady of Sorrows. The Spanish word for sorrows is "dolores," so people began calling the church Mission Dolores.
In 1782, the mission moved a short way to the west. A new adobe church was dedicated there in 1791. It is the same church that stands today.

For the Native people, the mission brought terrible loss. By 1801, all of the Native people of the San Francisco Peninsula had been brought into the mission. Sickness spread fast in the crowded rooms, and living and working there was very hard. By 1801, about eight out of every ten Ramaytush people had died. In 1795, a large group of people from across the bay ran away from the mission.

As the years passed, people from other tribes around the bay were brought to the mission too. When the government took the mission away from the Church in 1834, only 136 Native people still lived there. About 5,000 Native people are buried in the mission cemetery, most in graves with no markers.
In 1906, a great earthquake shook San Francisco. The big brick church next door was ruined, but the little adobe church was not harmed.
Today, only one Ramaytush family line is known to have living descendants. They lead a group called the Association of Ramaytush Ohlone. They care for the land and teach others about their people.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Ramaytush (say it rah-my-toosh) Ohlone, the first people of the San Francisco Peninsula. The local tribe at San Francisco is called the Yelamu today. No one knows what name they used for themselves. The National Park Service says that sickness and poor living and working conditions at the mission killed most of the Ramaytush people, and that by 1850 only about five Ramaytush families were still living. Later, people from other Native nations around the bay were also brought here, so the mission held people who spoke many different languages. The mission's own website says the cemetery is the resting place of about 5,000 Ohlone, Miwok, and other first Californians. The Ramaytush people who are living today say that they lost most of their culture and language, and they are working to care for their homeland once more.
type_specific.mission_life: The buildings around the mission courtyard were finished in 1798. People from many different tribes lived there close together. The rooms were crowded, and there was no separate place for people who were ill, so sickness passed quickly from one person to the next. Native people did the building, farming, and other work of the mission. For them it was a very different life from the one they had known in their own villages.
type_specific.architecture: The adobe church is 114 feet long and only 22 feet wide, with walls four feet thick. Look up, and you will see the most famous part. The ceiling beams are made of redwood, and they were tied together with strips of rawhide instead of nails. The beams are painted with bright Native designs. This church is the real one from 1791. It has not been rebuilt. Steel supports were added in 1917 to make it stronger, and more repairs were made after an earthquake in 1989. The large church next door, called Mission Dolores Basilica, is much newer.
